This is Subli. 18th century or earlier.

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance originated in Bauan and Alitagtag, Batangas.
Its birth is tied to the legend of a gambler husband who followed his wife to a spring beneath a cross-shaped tree, where a blinding light caused him to repent.
Music scholars suggest the frenetic drum rhythms reflect prehispanic animist origins adapted into Catholic devotion.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Performed during the Feast of the Mahal na Poon on May 3, birthdays, graduations, and healing rituals on any day except Lent, primarily to fulfill a panata (sacred negotiation).
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Performed in pairs by men and women called manunublî in various formations.
Male dancers maintain a distinct bent and stooped posture derived from the Tagalog words subsób and balî.
Women use straw hats adorned with ribbons, waving, removing, or tipping them in salute to an altar cross.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Accompanied by the constant beating of drums and the clacking of wooden castanets (kalaste) played by men.
Performances often begin with women chanting in archaic metaphorical language (talinghaga).
Listen for the drums, wooden castanets (kalaste), rondalla ensemble.
Constant beating of drums punctuated by the clacking of wooden castanets, accompanied by women chanting in an archaic metaphorical language.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Juan P. Silos composed the rondalla tune used for theatrical versions of the dance.
Regional variants include the Agoncillo version, the Sinala version (considered the original style using the tagunggo mode), and the Talumpok version.
A Christianized version of older, prehispanic animist rites, maintaining ties to the tagunggo musical mode while integrated into Catholic devotion to the Holy Cross.
